{{Short description|Family of polynomials}}
In [[algebra]], the '''Swinnerton-Dyer polynomials''' are a family of polynomials, introduced by [[Peter Swinnerton-Dyer]], that serve as examples where [[polynomial factorization]] algorithms have worst-case runtime.  They have the property of being [[reducible polynomial|reducible]] [[modulo]] every prime, while being irreducible over the rational numbers.  They are a standard counterexample in [[number theory]].

Given a finite set <math>P</math> of [[prime number]]s, the Swinnerton-Dyer polynomial associated to <math>P</math> is the polynomial:
<math display="block">f_P(x) = \prod \left(x + \sum_{p\in P} (\pm) \sqrt{p}\right)</math>
where the product extends over all <math>2^{|P|}</math> choices of sign in the enclosed sum.  The polynomial <math>f_P(x)</math> has degree <math>2^{|P|}</math> and integer coefficients, which alternate in sign.  If <math>|P|>1</math>, then <math>f_P(x)</math> is [[reducible polynomial|reducible]] modulo <math>p</math> for all primes <math>p</math>, into linear and quadratic factors, but irreducible over <math>\mathbb Q</math>.  The [[Galois group]] of <math>f_P(x)</math> is <math>\mathbb Z_2^{|P|}</math>.

The first few Swinnerton-Dyer polynomials are:
<math display="block">f_{\{2\}}(x) = x^2-2 = (x-\sqrt 2)(x+\sqrt 2)</math>
<math display="block">f_{\{2,3\}}(x) = x^4-10x^2+1 = (x-\sqrt 2-\sqrt 3)(x-\sqrt 2+\sqrt 3)(x+\sqrt 2 -\sqrt 3)(x+\sqrt 2+\sqrt 3)</math>
<math display="block">f_{\{2,3,5\}}(x) = x^8-40x^6+352x^4-960x^2+576.</math>
